key_insight: This study audits which mental health interventions 41 language models recommend when the same clinical case is presented by a clinician, caregiver, or patient. The provided abstract describes the audit but does not report whether recommendations differed across these roles.
problem_solved: How can researchers systematically assess whether language models' mental health recommendations depend on who is asking, even when the clinical information stays the same?
method: Presented 19 clinical case vignettes from three perspectives: clinician, caregiver, and patient.
Collected 35,055 free-text responses from 41 language models across five questions and extracted every named intervention using a validated judge.
Had 29 models rate the full list of intervention options.
impact: The audit provides a framework for evaluating role-sensitive behavior in mental health AI. Practitioners can use this approach to investigate recommendation consistency and potential safety concerns before deployment.
visual_elements: Three-lane diagram showing the same clinical case framed by a clinician, caregiver, and patient.
Audit pipeline: case vignettes → model responses → intervention extraction → option ratings.
Scale tiles highlighting 41 models, 19 vignettes, five questions, and 35,055 responses.
Illustrative comparison-matrix template for interventions across user roles, clearly labeled as a framework rather than reported results.
paper_title: Curbside Chatbots: Auditing the Mental Health Interventions Large Language Models Recommend to Clinicians, Caregivers, and Patients
paper_authors: Matthew Flathers, Jill Noorily, Phuong Anh Nguyen, Mark Kalinich, Mina Fallah
